narrative:
The model predicts you have a 19% chance of failing your final year, which is why the school is requiring you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your number of past class failures, your desire to pursue higher education, and how often you go out with friends. Past failures had the biggest impact and pushed the prediction toward failing. Even though you have had zero past failures—which matches the average for students who passed—this absence of prior setbacks still worked against you in the model’s logic, possibly because it made other risk factors stand out more.

Your strong ambition to continue into higher education worked in your favor and pulled the prediction toward passing. Almost every student who passes shares this same goal, so the model sees this as a clear positive signal.

How often you go out with friends was the third most important factor and also nudged the outcome toward failing. You spend a medium amount of time socializing, which is actually the most common pattern among students who ultimately pass, yet the model still interpreted this level of going out as increasing your risk.

To improve, focus on turning your ambition into concrete daily study habits and consider whether your social time is cutting into revision. Small, consistent changes in how you manage free time could lower your risk and help you pass without needing extra courses. (218 words)
